etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English senden, from Old English sendan (“to send, cause to go”), from Proto-West Germanic *sandijan, from Proto-Germanic *sandijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sont-eye- (“to cause to go”), causative of *sent- (“to walk, travel”). The noun is from the verb.

definitions.definition: (transitive, ditransitive) To make something (such as an object or message) go from one place to another (or to someone).

quote.citation: 2013 June 14, Jonathan Freedland, “Obama's once hip brand is now tainted”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 189, number 1, page 18:
quote.text: Now we are liberal with our innermost secrets, spraying them into the public ether with a generosity our forebears could not have imagined. Where we once sent love letters in a sealed envelope, or stuck photographs of our children in a family album, now such private material is despatched to servers and clouds operated by people we don't know and will never meet.

definitions.definition: (transitive, slang) To get one going; move to excitement or rapture; to delight or thrill.

quote.citation: 1947, Robertson Davies, The Diary of Samuel Marchbanks, Clarke, Irwin & Co., page 183:
quote.text: The train had an excellent whistle which sent me, just as Sinatra sends the bobby-sockers.

quote.citation: 1957, Sam Cooke, You Send Me:
quote.text: Darling you send me / I know you send me

quote.citation: 1991, P.M. Dawn, Set Adrift on Memory Bliss:
quote.text: Baby you send me.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To bring to a certain condition.

quote.citation: 1913, D[avid] H[erbert] Lawrence, “chapter 9”, in Sons and Lovers, London: Duckworth & Co. […], →OCLC:
quote.text: “I suppose,” blurted Clara suddenly, “she wants a man.”The other two were silent for a few moments.“But it’s the loneliness sends her cracked,” said Paul.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, usually with for) To dispatch an agent or messenger to convey a message or do an errand.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, 2 Kings vi:32:
quote.text: See ye how this son of a murderer hath sent to take away my head?

definitions.definition: (archaic, of a blessing or reward) To bestow; to grant.

quote.citation: c. 1604–1605 (date written), William Shakespeare, “All’s Well, that Ends Well”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i]:
quote.text: God send him well!

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Matthew 5:45:
quote.text: That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.

quote.citation: 1668, Izaak Walton, “Observations of the Otter and Chub”, in The Compleat Angler:
quote.text: Let’s be going with all my heart. God keep you all, Gentlemen, and send you meet this day with another Bitch-Otter, and kill her merrily, and all her young ones too.

quote.citation: c. 1700s, God Save the King:
quote.text: Send him victorious, / Happy and glorious, / Long to reign over us: / God save the King!

quote.citation: 1814 July 7, [Walter Scott], Waverley; or, ’Tis Sixty Years Since. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), Edinburgh:  […] James Ballantyne and Co. for Archibald Constable and Co.; London: Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown, →OCLC:
quote.text: God send your mission may bring back peace.

quote.citation: 1840–1841, Charles Dickens, chapter 68, in The Old Curiosity Shop:
quote.text: Good night, and Heaven send our journey may have a prosperous ending!

definitions.definition: (archaic, of a curse or punishment) To inflict; to visit.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Deuteronomy 28:20:
quote.text: The Lord shall send upon thee cursing, vexation, and rebuke.

quote.citation: 1884, Thomas Henry Huxley, William Jay Youmans, “Scope and Aims of Hygiene”, in The Elements of Physiology and Hygiene, page 345:
quote.text: Vague notions of this kind still widely prevail, and great numbers regard diseases as things that come arbitrarily, or are "sent" by Divine Providence as judgments or punishments for sins.

definitions.definition: (transitive, sometimes followed by a dependent proposition) To cause to be or to happen; to bring; bring about.
(climbing, transitive) To climb a route without falling.
(Nigeria, slang, intransitive) To care. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
(UK, slang) To call out or diss a specific person in a diss track.

quote.citation: 2017 November 7, “Courtney Jade Reply (Freestyle)”‎[1]performed by Soph Aspin:
quote.text: But if you want beef, it's war. I'll rip you to shreds and send once more […] And you think you can send for Aspin? Sort it, stop gassing.

definitions.definition: (Singapore, transitive) To give (someone) a lift, to drive (someone) to another place.

quote.citation: 2001 October 15, MPH Rubin (Judge), quoting Khwan-On Nathaphon, “Public Prosecutor v Khwan-On Nathaphon”, in elitigation.sg‎[2] (Judgment Text, CC 4/2001, Exhibit P-131 - statement recorded on 15 June 2000), High Court of Singapore, retrieved 12 December 2024:
quote.text: […]  After closing the door, I shifted to the extreme right and sat directly behind the taxi driver. I told the driver to send me to Pasir Ris by saying "Pasir Ris Dr 12", bus stop"  […]

definitions.definition: (telecommunications) An operation in which data is transmitted.

quote.citation: 1992, Tara M. Madhyastha, A Portable System for Data Sonification, page 71:
quote.text: In the sonification of the PDE code, notes are scattered throughout a wide pitch range, and sends and receives are relatively balanced; although in the beginning of the application there are bursts of sends  […]

definitions.definition: (graphical user interface; often capitalized, or capitalized and put in quotation marks) An icon (usually on a computer screen and labeled with the word "Send") on which one clicks (with a mouse or its equivalent) or taps to transmit an email or other electronic message.

quote.citation: 1877, William Clark Russell, The Frozen Pirate:
quote.text: thus we drifted, steadily trending with the send of each giant surge further and deeper into the icy regions of the south-west

quote.citation: 1858 October 16, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, “The Courtship of Miles Standish”, in The Courtship of Miles Standish, and Other Poems, Boston, Mass.: Ticknor and Fields, →OCLC:
quote.text: the send of the sea

quote.citation: 1886 October – 1887 January, H[enry] Rider Haggard, She: A History of Adventure, London: Longmans, Green, and Co., published 1887, →OCLC:
quote.text: The send of the sea was driving the boat's head round to starboard.

definitions.definition: (Scotland) A messenger, especially one sent to fetch the bride.
(UK, slang) A callout or diss usually aimed at a specific person, often in the form of a diss track.

quote.citation: 2017 November 7, “Courtney Jade Reply (Freestyle)”‎[3]performed by Soph Aspin:
quote.text: Why you're another bird that's fat again. No competition that's, that's the send.

definitions.definition: (climbing) A successful ascent of a sport climbing route.
